sections.b: No book of wisdom says more about the tongue than Sirach, and chapters 19-23 are its densest stretch. Ben Sira tells his pupils to keep what they hear to themselves ("Let it die with you", 19:10), to check a story with the person it is about before acting on it, because "slander is common" (19:13-17), and to learn the timing of speech: one person keeps quiet because he has nothing to say, another because he knows the right moment (20:5-7). A slip of the tongue is worse than a fall on the floor (20:18), a habitual liar is worse than a thief (20:25), and the whisperer stains his own soul (21:28). The section ends with a prayer for "a guard at my mouth" (22:27, from Psalm 141:3) and a lesson titled "Discipline for the mouth" on careless oaths, coarse talk and insults (23:7-15). James 3 is the New Testament's nearest parallel.

common: Sirach teaches that a careless word can do more harm than a physical fall (Sirach 20:18).

sections.b: Ben Sira separates quarrels from betrayal. "If you draw a sword against a friend, / do not give up hope", and angry words can be mended too; but "taunting and arrogance, / telling a secret and a treacherous blow" drive any friend away (Sirach 22:21-22). The Hebrew of Genizah MS C turns the first two lines into commands, "Do not draw a sword ... for there is atonement", "Do not open your mouth ... for there is repentance". He tells his pupils to be loyal to a friend while he is poor and to stand by him in trouble (22:23), and not to be ashamed to shelter him (22:25). Insults drive friends away like a stone thrown at birds (22:20). He returns to secrets at 27:16-21 and to false friends at 6:5-17 and 37:1-6.

Chapters 19-23 of Sirach are mostly practical advice, but the fear of the Lord frames them. "All wisdom is the fear of the Lord, / and all wisdom includes doing what the law says" (19:20). "Better to fall short in understanding and fear God / than to be rich in good sense and break the law" (19:24). Wisdom is "the fear of the Lord brought to completion" (21:11). And after the warnings against adultery, "those who remain will come to know / that nothing is better than the fear of the Lord" (23:27). Manners, silence and loyalty count as wisdom only when they grow from reverence for God, as Proverbs 1:7 and Job 28:28 teach.
sections.refs: Sirach 19:20; Sirach 19:24; Sirach 21:11; Sirach 23:27; Proverbs 1:7; Job 28:28

sections.b: Ben Sira warns that cleverness is not wisdom. "Knowing how to do evil is not wisdom" (19:22); there is "a shrewdness that is exact, yet unjust" (19:25), and a shrewdness "that piles up bitterness" (21:12). True wisdom is known by its fruit: the wise man's knowledge swells like a flood and his advice is a spring of life, while the fool's mind is a cracked jar (21:13-14). Discipline is chains to the fool and a gold ornament to the sensible (21:19, 21). Hidden wisdom helps no one (20:30), which Jesus' sayings about the lamp and the buried talent echo (Matthew 5:15; Matthew 25:25).

"The ungodly man who curses Satan / is cursing his own soul" (Sirach 21:27). The Greek ton satanan may mean the devil, so that a sinner who blames the tempter is still answerable for his own choice, a point Ben Sira makes about blaming God in 15:11-12. It may mean a human adversary, as the Hebrew satan does in 1 Kings 11:14, so that a curse on an enemy rebounds. And it may be read with the later rabbinic saying that "Satan, the evil inclination, and the Angel of Death are one" (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 16a), so that cursing Satan is cursing one's own impulses. The Hebrew of the verse is lost.

Sirach 22:1-2 uses the Greek word of Proverbs for the lazy one (oknēros, Proverbs 6:6) but trades Proverbs' humor for disgust: he is "like a stone smeared with filth", and "like a lump of dung from the manure pile: / whoever picks it up will shake his hand clean". Codex Sinaiticus and the Latin have "is stoned with" instead of "is like", a picture of public scorn. In Ben Sira's honor culture, the neighbors' hissing was itself the punishment.

Ben Sira does not forbid oaths, but he warns against the habit of swearing and of "naming the Holy One" (Sirach 23:9). A man who swears all the time cannot stay clean, as a slave who is always under the whip cannot stay unbruised (23:10); a careless oath that is broken is sin, ignoring it doubles the sin, and a false oath fills his house with troubles (23:11). The Hebrew of Genizah MS C survives for 23:11: "A man of oaths will be filled with guilt, and the plague will not depart from his house." Jesus goes further: "do not take oaths at all" (Matthew 5:34).

sections.h: The eyes that see in the dark (Sirach 23:18-20)
sections.b: The adulterer of Sirach 23:18 says, "Who sees me? / Darkness is all around me; the walls keep me covered". Ben Sira answers that "the eyes of the Lord / are ten thousand times brighter than the sun" and "peer into the secret places" (23:19), and that all things were known to God before they were created (23:20). The same book insists that people choose freely and cannot blame God (15:11-20), so his teaching on God's knowledge is never an excuse. Compare Proverbs 15:3, Psalm 139:11-12 and Hebrews 4:13.
sections.refs: Sirach 23:18-20; Sirach 15:11-20; Proverbs 15:3; Psalm 139:11-16; Hebrews 4:13; Job 24:15

sections.b: Sirach 23:16-27 condemns both partners in adultery. The man who "strays from his own bed" thinks no one sees and "will be punished in the city squares" (23:18-21). The wife who "deserts her husband / and provides an heir fathered by a stranger" has broken God's law, wronged her husband and corrupted his line (23:22-23); she is brought before the assembly, and her memory is cursed (23:24-26). The law of Moses called for death for both (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22); Ben Sira names public punishment but no court penalty. His harsh words on her children (23:25) stand in tension with Ezekiel 18:20.
sections.refs: Sirach 23:16-27; Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22; Proverbs 6:32-35; Ezekiel 18:20; Matthew 5:27-28; John 8:3-11

sections.b: Ben Sira says "It is a father's shame to have fathered an undisciplined son, / and a daughter is born to his loss" (Sirach 22:3), then sets a sensible daughter who gains a husband against a brazen one who shames father and husband (22:4-5). "Whippings and discipline are wisdom in every season" (22:6), as Proverbs 13:24 says of the rod. Two lines found only in the longer Greek (22:9-10) add that good children cover a family's humble birth and proud ones soil its nobility. His fuller teaching on the rod is at 30:1-13. Readers differ on whether such verses command physical punishment or record the practice of an ancient culture.

Sirach's prayer for guarded lips addresses God twice as a personal Father: "Lord, Father and Master of my life" (23:1) and "Lord, Father and God of my life" (23:4). The Hebrew Bible calls God the Father of Israel (Isaiah 63:16; Isaiah 64:8) and of the king (Psalm 89:26), and Wisdom 14:3 prays "your providence, Father". In 51:10 the Greek of Sirach reads "the Lord, the father of my lord". Jesus teaches his followers to pray "Our Father" (Matthew 6:9). Codex Alexandrinus reads "God" for "Master" in 23:1. The Hebrew of these verses is lost.
sections.refs: Sirach 23:1; Sirach 23:4; Sirach 51:10; Isaiah 63:16; Isaiah 64:8; Psalm 89:26; Wisdom 14:3; Matthew 6:9

sections.b: A line found only in the longer Greek of Sirach, and so in the KJV, says that "those who do what pleases him pick fruit from the tree of immortality" (Sirach 19:19). It recalls the tree of life (Genesis 2:9; Revelation 2:7) and hopes for life beyond death, which the base text of Ben Sira does not promise (17:27-28; 41:4). The verse is missing from Codex Vaticanus and from the Latin; this site prints it in brackets, translated from codex 248.

sections.h: The law that masters the inclination (Sirach 21:11)
sections.b: "A man who keeps the law gets the upper hand over his thoughts" (Sirach 21:11). Ben Sira says in 15:14 that God left humanity in the power of its own inclination, the Hebrew yetser. The Talmud later has God say, "I created an evil inclination, ... and I created Torah as its antidote" (Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 30b), reading Genesis 4:7, "you must rule over it". Ben Sira already holds that obeying God's law trains the inner life.

Sirach warns that "the man who joins himself to prostitutes grows more reckless" (19:2), the same Greek phrase Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 6:16. In 23:16-17 he pictures lust as a fire that burns until it consumes, and a man "who commits sexual sin in the body of his own flesh", which may mean incest (compare Leviticus 18:6) or sin with his own body. In 23:23 the adulterous wife "in sexual sin" (en porneia) "has committed adultery", joining the two Greek words.
sections.refs: Sirach 19:2; Sirach 23:16-17; Sirach 23:23; 1 Corinthians 6:16-18; Leviticus 18:6; Proverbs 9:17
